back: Ethics is the philosophical study and system of principles of right and wrong; morality is the set of values and norms actually accepted in a society or culture.
The norms and duties of a specific profession (receptionist, waiter, guide) that go beyond general morality, e.g. confidentiality, honesty, food safety.

front: Why ethics matters especially in hospitality
back: Service is intangible and delivered face to face, guests are vulnerable away from home, staff access rooms and personal data, and reputation spreads fast online.
Personal (employee), professional (occupation), organisational (hotel, restaurant, tour operator), societal/global (industry, destinations, sustainability).
Consequence-based theory (Bentham, Mill): the right action brings the greatest good for the greatest number. Weakness: may sacrifice the minority.
Duty-based ethics (Kant): some actions are right or wrong in themselves; keep promises, tell the truth, treat people as ends, never merely as means.
Theory from Aristotle focusing on character: ask what a good, honest professional would do; develop virtues such as honesty, fairness and generosity.
Ethics as fairness: fair distribution of benefits and burdens and equal treatment; the 'veil of ignorance' thought experiment.

front: UNWTO Global Code of Ethics for Tourism
back: Ten voluntary principles for responsible tourism adopted by the UNWTO General Assembly in 1999 (Santiago, Chile), acknowledged by the UN General Assembly in 2001.

front: Code of ethics vs code of conduct
back: Code of ethics states values and principles (the 'why'); code of conduct gives concrete rules of behaviour for employees (what to do and not do).

front: What makes a corporate code effective?
back: Clear language, staff training, leaders following it, confidential reporting channel, protection of whistleblowers, fair sanctions, regular review.
Shared values, beliefs and habits in an organisation that put the guest's needs at the centre of every job.
Five dimensions of service quality: Reliability, Assurance, Tangibles, Empathy, Responsiveness (Parasuraman, Zeithaml, Berry).
Any contact in which a guest forms an impression of the company; term popularised by Jan Carlzon of SAS.
Giving front-line staff authority to solve guest problems on the spot without waiting for a manager.
Clean, complete uniform with name badge; neat hair; short clean nails; minimal jewellery; moderate make-up; no strong perfume; good personal hygiene.

front: Ethical limits of a dress code
back: Rules must relate to hygiene, safety or brand, apply equally to all, and respect religion, gender and disability where possible.
Answer quickly with a smile in the voice: greeting + hotel/department + own name + offer of help; repeat key details; let the guest hang up first.
Messages without words: facial expression, gestures, posture, eye contact, distance (proxemics) and tone. Crossed arms or using a phone show disrespect.

front: Replying to a negative online review
back: Reply promptly and politely, thank and apologise, explain what was changed, reveal no personal data, move details to a private channel.
Judging other cultures by the standards of one's own and seeing one's own as superior; a barrier to intercultural service.
Dastarkhan: the generously laid Kazakh festive table. Tör: the place of honour farthest from the entrance, given to the most respected guest or elder.
Kazakh tradition of hospitality: the guest is honoured, offered tea and the best food, even an unexpected traveller ('God's guest'), and given sarqyt to take home.
Listen, Empathize, Apologize, React, Notify — a complaint-handling model; Notify means informing the guest and colleagues so the problem is not repeated.
Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank — a short complaint-handling model.
A guest whose problem was solved very well may become more loyal than one who had no problem at all.
Accepting more bookings than rooms; walking = moving a confirmed guest to another hotel. Ethically: early warning, comparable room, pay first night and transport, fair criteria.
Never give room numbers or confirm a stay to third parties; say the room number quietly; respect 'Do not disturb'; protect passport and card data.
A situation where personal interests could influence professional decisions, e.g. a supplier's personal payment to a purchasing manager.
Tip: voluntary money from a guest. Service charge: fixed percentage added by the business; it should be clearly shown and, ethically, reach the staff.
Clear policy, training, safe reporting channels, panic buttons for room attendants, equal investigation for all and support for victims.
Leading with integrity, fairness and care; the leader is both a moral person and a moral manager who sets the 'tone at the top'.
Leadership approach (Robert Greenleaf) where the leader's first aim is to serve and develop employees, who then serve guests better.
Presenting a business as more environmentally friendly than it really is, e.g. an 'eco-hotel' label with no real measures.
Showing a low price first and adding compulsory fees (resort fee, taxes, service charge) only later in the booking process.
A situation where values or duties conflict and every option has a moral cost, e.g. loyalty to a colleague vs honesty to the employer.

front: Steps of an ethical decision model
back: Facts, ethical issue, stakeholders, options, evaluation (theories, law, code), decision and action, review.
Economic (be profitable), legal (obey the law), ethical (do what is fair), philanthropic (be a good corporate citizen).
Measuring business success by People, Planet and Profit (John Elkington).
Universal design: spaces usable by all without adaptation. Reasonable accommodation: necessary adjustments so a person with a disability can use a service.
